title: Pentecostal theology
hook: a theology of the Spirit, experience and empowerment

segments.voice: Yesterday, feminist and womanist voices: Hagar naming the God who sees. Your line was her story too. Which woman's story did you read, and what did she do? Day one thousand two hundred eighty.

A plain building on Azusa Street in Los Angeles. People crowd in to pray, and they stay late. The preacher is a Black man named William J. Seymour. Visitors carry stories away with them: people speaking in tongues, people healed, Black and white worshipers praising God in the same room. Some come to mock, and some come back to stay. Pentecostals tell their story through revivals like this one, and through older ones too. Today, a theology that grew from rooms like that: Pentecostal theology, and the power it talks about.

The name comes from Pentecost, the day in the book of Acts when the Holy Spirit comes on the disciples in Jerusalem. Before he leaves them, Jesus promises: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me." Then it happens. A sound like a rushing wind. Tongues like fire. The disciples speak, and visitors from far-off lands hear them in their own languages. Peter stands up and explains it with the prophet Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Pentecostal theology takes that day as a pattern, not only a memory. The Spirit, Pentecostals say, still comes with power: in worship, in healing, in gifts like speaking in tongues, and above all in boldness to tell others about Jesus. Notice the order in that promise. The power is for something. Ye shall receive power, and ye shall be witnesses. It isn't for show. Experience matters deeply here. Faith is not only believed; it is met. That's part of why Pentecostal worship can be loud and open, with raised hands, spoken prayer and testimony. Christians differ on these gifts. Some hold that tongues and prophecy continue today. Others believe they belonged to the time of the apostles. Others welcome the Spirit's work in quieter ways. And Paul, writing to a church full of these gifts, puts something above them all: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."

Here's the practice: ask for power to love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's hard for you to love right now. Don't force a warm feeling. Just hold them there. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for power to love that person today, in your own words, or with the old cry of the church, come, Holy Spirit. If you don't pray, ask yourself what one loving act toward them would look like. The bell holds the time.
Pentecostal theology. A theology of the Holy Spirit, met in experience and giving power to witness, named for the day of Pentecost in Acts.
Your line: power to witness. Today, tell one person, simply and honestly, about something good you've been given, and let it be true, not a sales pitch. Day one thousand two hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians worship with spoken and sung prayer, raised hands, testimony and prayer for healing, and pray for the gifts of the Spirit; other churches also mark the feast of Pentecost each year.

notes: Azusa Street: no dates given under the claims rule. Statements: a plain building on Azusa Street, Los Angeles; led by William J. Seymour, a Black preacher; reports of tongues and healing; Black and white worshipers together; 'some come to mock, and some come back to stay'. Confirm these are fair to the historical accounts.
'Pentecostals tell their story through revivals like this one, and through older ones too' avoids naming Azusa as the sole origin; confirm.
Cessationist and continuationist views summarized without ranking ('belonged to the time of the apostles'); confirm wording.
'Come, Holy Spirit' is described as an old cry of the church (Veni Sancte Spiritus / Veni Creator), not given as a full prayer.
howItsDone 'many pray for the gifts of the Spirit' refers to Pentecostal and charismatic Christians; soften to 'some' if preferred.
Editor pass: dropped the repeated 'this path ranks none of them' (teach and myth), used on the days just before.
No 'dynamite' etymology for dunamis, by design.

Audit (2026-10-02): no change. Acts 1:8, 2:17, 1 Corinthians 13:1 and the Azusa Street details checked; 'above all in boldness to tell others' is attributed to Pentecostals and matches the Acts 1:8 emphasis.
